model_answers.transcript:
I want to tell about a decision I made about three years ago. At that time I am working in a small company, only nine people, and another company offered me a job.

The other job was better. The salary was more, maybe twenty percent more, and the office was near to my home, only twenty minutes. So it was a good offer, and everybody told me to take it. My mother said take it, my friends said take it also.

But I decided to stay in my company. Because in my company I have a manager and she is very good, she teaches me many things. And in the big company I don't know anybody, and I think maybe I am only a number for them.

So I said no to them. It was difficult, and for two months I feel bad about the money. But after six months my manager gives me a big project alone, and now I am a team leader. So it was good. If I take that job, maybe I am not a team leader now. So I think money is not everything, and this is my decision that turned out well.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a decision I made about three years ago, which was turning down a job that would have paid me quite a bit more.

At the time I was working for a small firm — nine of us, all in one room — and a much bigger company got in touch and offered me a role. On paper it was an easy call. The salary was around twenty per cent higher, the office was twenty minutes from my flat rather than an hour, and not one person I asked told me to stay.

What made me hesitate was my manager. She'd taught me most of what I actually know how to do, and she was still handing me work I wasn't quite ready for, which is how you learn anything. At the bigger place I'd have been one of about forty people doing the same job. So it came down to money against the person I was learning from, and in the end that's what tipped the balance.

Turning it down was harder than I expected, and for the first couple of months I did wonder whether I'd been sentimental about it. Then, about six months later, she put me in charge of a project on my own, and I'm now running a small team, whereas if I'd moved I'd probably still be doing the same tasks I was doing back then. Looking back, I'd say the useful part wasn't the decision itself — it was working out that I was choosing what I'd be taught, not just where I'd sit.

'On paper', 'tipped the balance', 'got in touch' — chunks carry the meaning, not adjectives.
Two signposted moves, and a close that names what was learned rather than the card.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one step further
model_answers.transcript:
This was three years ago, and it was a decision to turn something down rather than to take it — an offer that was, on the face of it, plainly better than what I already had.

I was at a small firm then, nine of us in a single room, and a far larger company approached me. Twenty per cent more money, a twenty-minute commute instead of an hour, and not one person I consulted advised me against it. What nobody could see from outside was that most of the value of the job I was in sat with one person — the manager who'd trained me, and who was still quietly handing me work I hadn't earned yet. That is a rare thing, and it isn't advertised anywhere.

So the choice wasn't really money against loyalty. It was whether I was picking a salary or picking who I'd be taught by, and once I'd put it in those terms it more or less made itself.

It was still uncomfortable. For a couple of months I half-suspected I'd dressed up cold feet as principle. Then, six months in, she handed me a project of my own, and I've run a small team ever since. Had I taken the offer, I'd almost certainly have ended up competent and interchangeable, which is a worse place to be at that age than underpaid. What I take from it now is that the decisions people call good ones are rarely the ones with the better numbers attached — they're the ones where somebody managed to work out what they were actually choosing between.

model_answers.transcript:
I would like to talk about a change I made two years ago. I moved out from my parents' house and I go to live alone in a small flat.

Before, I am living with my parents, my two sisters and my grandmother. It was a full house and very noisy, but also comfortable, because my mother cooks and everything is done for me. And I was twenty-four, and many of my friends already moved out before me.

The change was in September two years ago. I found a flat in the other side of the city, near to my work. It is one room and a kitchen only, but it is mine.

It affected my mother the most. She was sad and she called me every day in the first month. My sisters were happy because they get my room.

The difference is that now I do everything myself, cooking and bills and cleaning. In the beginning it was very hard and I was going home every weekend. But now it is good and I am more independent person. So this is the important change of my life.

what_caps_it.point: The narrative drops into the present five times, and two articles are missing.
Facts arrive in a list joined by 'and', and the close reads the card back.
'Good', 'hard', 'sad', 'happy', 'comfortable' — every judgement is a bare adjective.

annotations.span: The change was in September two years ago.
annotations.label: Dates the change plainly
annotations.why: Keep this — a month and a year anchor the whole tense for the listener.

annotations.span: I go to live alone in a small flat
annotations.label: Present tense inside a past story
annotations.why: 'I went to live on my own' — decide the tense in sentence one.

annotations.span: Before, I am living with my parents
annotations.label: The 'before' needs a past form
annotations.why: 'Up until then I'd lived with my parents' shows two layers of time.

annotations.span: in the other side of the city
annotations.label: Wrong preposition in a fixed phrase
annotations.why: It is 'on the other side of'. Learn the preposition inside the chunk.

annotations.span: I am more independent person
annotations.label: Article missing before a singular noun
annotations.why: 'I'm a more independent person.' Countable singular always takes a determiner.

annotations.span: So this is the important change of my life.
annotations.label: Ends by repeating the prompt
annotations.why: Finish with what the change taught you, not with the card's wording.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a change I made a couple of years ago, which was moving out of my parents' house and getting a place of my own.

Up until then I'd lived at home my whole life — my parents, my two sisters and my grandmother, all in one house. It was noisy in a way I actually liked, and to be honest most things were done for me. But I was twenty-four by then, most of the people I'd been at university with had already moved out, and I'd started to feel slightly stuck.

So in the September of that year I took the plunge and rented a small flat on the other side of the city, about ten minutes from where I work. It's one room and a kitchen, and the rent takes a third of what I earn, but it's mine.

The person it affected most wasn't me — it was my mother. She rang every single day for about a month, and I think she read the move as a verdict on the house rather than a decision about me, which it honestly wasn't.

As for the difference it's made, the obvious answer is that I've had to learn how to run a household, and that's true enough. But the thing I hadn't expected was how much better I get on with my family now that I see them once a week instead of every evening. In hindsight, the distance turned out to be the point rather than the price.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect builds a before-and-after that band 6 flattened into one tense.
'Took the plunge', 'read the move as a verdict', 'in hindsight' carry the evaluation.
The fourth bullet is signposted, and the close is an insight, not a summary.

annotations.span: Up until then I'd lived at home my whole life
annotations.label: Past perfect opens the 'before'
annotations.why: One 'I'd + participle' at the start does the whole background for you.

annotations.span: It was noisy in a way I actually liked
annotations.label: Qualifies instead of judging flatly
annotations.why: Adding 'in a way that…' turns an adjective into an observation.

annotations.span: most of the people I'd been at university with had already moved out
annotations.label: Two past perfects justify the decision
annotations.why: Use the form to show what was already true when you acted.

annotations.span: I took the plunge
annotations.label: One idiom, exactly where it belongs
annotations.why: Save it for the moment you finally did the thing you'd delayed.

annotations.span: The person it affected most wasn't me — it was my mother.
annotations.label: Cleft sentence turns the answer
annotations.why: 'The one who ___ wasn't ___, it was ___' reorganises a whole bullet.

annotations.span: she read the move as a verdict on the house rather than a decision about me
annotations.label: A precise contrast, not a rare word
annotations.why: 'X rather than Y' lets you say exactly what somebody misunderstood.

annotations.span: As for the difference it's made
annotations.label: Announces the last bullet aloud
annotations.why: Saying the move out loud stops you running out of time before it.

annotations.span: the thing I hadn't expected was how much better I get on with my family
annotations.label: Names an unplanned consequence
annotations.why: An unexpected result always sounds real; a planned one sounds rehearsed.

annotations.span: In hindsight, the distance turned out to be the point rather than the price.
annotations.label: Closes above the anecdote
annotations.why: One retrospective sentence lifts the turn out of pure narration.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one step further
model_answers.transcript:
The change I'd pick is moving out of my parents' house, which I did a couple of years back and which took me far longer to get round to than it should have.

I'd lived in that house since I was born — two parents, two sisters, a grandmother, and never a quiet room in it. I don't want to make it sound like an escape, because it wasn't; the noise was half of what I liked about the place. But at twenty-four I was still being looked after, and there comes a point at which being looked after starts to feel like being held still.

I rented a flat on the far side of the city that September, ten minutes from work, one room and a kitchen, with a rent that swallows a third of what I bring in. Modest, but entirely my own.

What I hadn't reckoned with was my mother. She phoned daily for a month, and I gradually worked out that she'd taken the move as a comment on the house rather than a decision about me — which is a distinction that is almost impossible to explain to somebody while they're upset.

The difference it's made isn't really the domestic competence, though I've had to pick that up. It's that seeing my family once a week rather than every evening has done more for how we get on than fifteen years of living on top of each other ever managed. Only with a bit of distance did any of us become particularly easy to like.

what_lifts_it.point: Negative inversion at the close, where band 7 used an ordinary statement.
'Get round to', 'reckoned with', 'swallows a third' sit naturally, undisplayed.
It heads off the wrong reading of the story before making its point.

annotations.span: took me far longer to get round to than it should have
annotations.label: A phrasal verb doing precise work
annotations.why: 'Get round to' says delayed-not-refused in three words.

annotations.span: being looked after starts to feel like being held still
annotations.label: Reframes the situation in one image
annotations.why: One line of interpretation is worth thirty seconds of extra detail.

annotations.span: What I hadn't reckoned with was my mother.
annotations.label: Cleft plus past perfect together
annotations.why: Combining two structures in one short sentence is what sustained control looks like.

annotations.span: she'd taken the move as a comment on the house rather than a decision about me
annotations.label: Precision about somebody else's reading
annotations.why: Reporting a misunderstanding exactly is harder — and worth more — than describing an emotion.

annotations.span: Modest, but entirely my own.
annotations.label: A short sentence breaks the rhythm
annotations.why: Drop your pitch and pause before it; the contrast does the emphasis.

annotations.span: Only with a bit of distance did any of us become particularly easy to like.
annotations.label: Negative inversion after 'only'
annotations.why: 'Only after ___ did I ___' is the one inversion worth drilling for speech.

model_answers.transcript:
I will talk about my achievement. I finish a teaching qualification two years ago and I am very proud about this.

It was a part-time course, so I am working in the day and studying in the evening, and also on Saturday sometimes. It took two years. It was very hard because I am tired all the time and I don't sleep enough.

In the first year I failed my first lesson. A teacher came and she watched me for forty minutes and after she said it is not good enough. I was very sad and I want to stop the course. But my friend said to me, try one more time. So after three months I try again and this time I passed.

Not many people knew about it. I didn't tell my family because I think maybe I will fail again. Only my friend knew. My mother knew at the end when I finished and she cried.

It mattered because I never think that I can do this. In my family nobody is a teacher. So it was a very big thing for me. So this is my achievement that I am proud of.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about finishing a teaching qualification, which I did about two years ago and which took me the best part of two years to get through.

It was a part-time course, so I was working during the day and studying most evenings and every other Saturday. That sounds manageable said out loud, but by around the fourth month I was permanently tired and I'd more or less stopped seeing anybody.

The part I'd point to is what happened in the first year. You have to be observed teaching a full lesson, and my first observation went badly — the assessor sat at the back for forty minutes and then told me, perfectly politely, that it wasn't good enough. I remember walking home afterwards and deciding I'd hand the whole thing in. A friend on the same course talked me out of it, and I did the observation again three months later and got through it.

Hardly anybody knew I was doing it, actually. I hadn't told my family, mainly because I'd convinced myself I'd fail and I didn't fancy explaining that twice. My mother found out on the day I finished, and she cried, which I wasn't remotely prepared for.

As for why it mattered — I think because nobody in my family had done anything like it, so I genuinely had no idea whether I could. Passing the second observation told me more than the certificate did. In a way the qualification is the least interesting part; what I came away with was evidence that I don't fold the first time something goes wrong.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect and a proper reported-speech backshift replace the present-tense slips.
'The best part of two years', 'talked me out of it', 'I don't fold' carry it.
The setback is announced as the centre of the story, and the close reinterprets it.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one step further
model_answers.transcript:
The thing I'd choose is a teaching qualification I finished a couple of years ago, taken part-time over two years while I was working.

On paper that's a single sentence. In practice it was most evenings and every other Saturday for the best part of twenty-four months, and by the spring of the first year I'd stopped being much use to anybody, including myself.

What made it an achievement rather than simply a slog was the first observation. Somebody sits at the back of your classroom for forty minutes and then tells you, very courteously, that what you did was not good enough — and there's no arguing with it, because they happen to be right. I walked home that evening having quietly decided to withdraw. A friend on the course sat me down and pointed out that I was treating one bad hour as a verdict on two years. Three months later I was observed again and got through it comfortably.

Almost nobody knew I was doing it. I hadn't told my family, on the grounds that failing privately is a good deal cheaper than failing in public, and my mother only learned about it the week I finished.

Looking back, the certificate is the least of it. What I came away with was a piece of evidence about myself I couldn't have obtained any other way — that a bad first attempt is information rather than a verdict. Had I withdrawn that evening, I'd have spent years believing something about myself that wasn't true.

what_lifts_it.point: A perfect participle clause and an inversion where band 7 used ordinary past forms.
'A slog', 'no arguing with it', 'the least of it' arrive without being shown off.
It defines what turned effort into achievement, then closes on a general claim.

I want to talk about a mistake in my work. Last year I am organising a small event for our company and I made the leaflets with the wrong date on them.

I was working in the marketing department and it was my second month there. My manager asked me to print eight hundred leaflets for the event. I write the text myself, and I send it to the printer. But I copy the top part from the old leaflet from the last event, so the date was the old date.

Nobody sees this problem, also not me. The boxes came and we put the leaflets in the library and in two shops. After two days a woman phoned and she asked which date is correct. I felt terrible. We must print everything again and it costs about four hundred euros.

My manager was not angry but she was disappointing, I think. She said next time show me first.

Now I always check with another person before I send something, even a small email. So this is my mistake and what I learn from it.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a mistake I made at work last year, which was sending eight hundred leaflets to the printer with the wrong date on them.

I'd been in the marketing team about two months, so I was still at the stage of trying to look competent. We were running a small open day, and my manager asked me to get the leaflets designed and printed. I wrote the text myself, and to save time I copied the header from the leaflet we'd used for the previous event — which of course still had the previous event's date sitting in it.

Nobody spotted it, including me. The boxes arrived, we dropped them off at the library and a couple of shops, and it wasn't until two days later that a member of the public rang up to ask which date was right. Reprinting cost about four hundred euros and, worse, we'd already put the wrong date in front of a few hundred people.

What I'd braced myself for was being shouted at. What actually happened was that my manager said, fairly mildly, that she'd rather have seen it before it went out, which was a good deal harder to hear than shouting would have been.

What I do differently now is dull but effective: nothing with a date, a price or a name in it leaves my desk until somebody else has read it. It takes four minutes. And I'd argue the real mistake wasn't copying the header — it was assuming that being quick and being careful were the same thing.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one step further
model_answers.transcript:
The one I'd pick is small and entirely avoidable: about a year ago, eight hundred leaflets went to the printer carrying the date of an event that had already taken place.

I'd been in the team a couple of months and was still at the stage of wanting to look quick rather than careful. We had an open day coming up and, instead of building the leaflet from scratch, I lifted the header off the previous one and changed what I thought needed changing. The date was not on that list.

Nobody caught it — not the printer, not my manager, and least of all me. The boxes went out to a library and two shops, and it took a phone call from a member of the public, forty-eight hours later, to establish that several hundred people had been given the wrong information. The reprint came to roughly four hundred euros, which was the cheap part.

What I'd steeled myself for was being taken apart. What I got was my manager remarking, quite mildly, that she'd have liked to see it first — and mild disappointment turns out to be considerably more effective than anger.

Nothing with a date or a price on it now leaves my desk unread by somebody else. It costs four minutes. And the useful lesson had nothing to do with proofreading: speed and care had felt like the same virtue to me, and they are not remotely the same thing.

what_lifts_it.point: A passive with a perfect infinitive and an 'it took X to Y' structure carry the aftermath.
'Taken apart', 'the cheap part', 'steeled myself' land without being displayed.

I'll talk about a plan I've had for about a year now, which is to go and work abroad — probably Ireland, possibly Canada — within the next two years.

The idea really started with my cousin. He moved to Ireland three years ago and he's been working in a hospital there ever since, and when he came home last summer he said, fairly bluntly, that there was nothing actually stopping me doing the same. I'd assumed the whole thing was complicated in a way it apparently isn't, so that conversation is what set it off.

So far I've done three things. I've been putting money aside every month since January — about four thousand at this point, which is roughly half of what I'd need. I'm doing this exam, obviously, which is the one part of it I can't hurry. And I've sent off the first stage of the registration paperwork, which everybody warns me will take the best part of a year to come back.

The plan I'd describe is a fairly ordinary one: to be working abroad inside two years — Ireland most likely, Canada if that falls through.

It crystallised about a year ago, and I can date it to a single conversation. A cousin of mine has been working in a hospital in Dublin since he left, and when he was home last summer he pointed out, not especially gently, that the only thing keeping me here was my own assumption that it would be difficult. He was right, which was irritating.

Since then I've been chipping away at it. Money first — I've put by roughly four thousand, which covers about half of what the move would genuinely cost. This exam, obviously. And the registration paperwork, the first stage of which has gone in and which I'm told will take the better part of a year to come back.

What sits underneath it is that I've lived in one city my entire life, and I'd sooner discover at twenty-six whether I can manage somewhere else than spend my forties wondering. My mother would rather I stayed, and I don't think she's wrong to feel that; I just don't think it's a reason. I'll talk about a piece of advice my first manager gave me, which I got when I was about twenty-three and which I still think about.

At that point I'd been in the job maybe six months and I was pretty nervous in meetings. What I'd got into the habit of doing was apologising before I said anything — sorry, this might be a silly question, sorry, I'm probably wrong about this. I wasn't even aware I was doing it.

She called me over one afternoon, perfectly pleasantly, and she asked me why I kept saying sorry before I opened my mouth, which I hadn't expected at all. Then she said something that landed: when you apologise first, people stop listening to the idea and start listening to the apology. Which was uncomfortable, because it was so obviously true.

What I did about it was fairly mechanical. For roughly two months I wrote the word 'sorry' at the top of my notebook before every meeting, purely so that I'd catch myself. I still slipped up constantly for the first few weeks, but by about the spring of that year it had more or less gone.

The difference it made wasn't really about meetings at all. It was that I'd been treating my own opinions as things that needed apologising for, and once somebody had pointed that out I couldn't stop seeing it. I'd say the best advice I've been given has all been like that — not new information, just somebody naming a habit I was too close to notice.

The piece of advice I keep coming back to came from my first manager, when I was twenty-three and roughly six months into the job.

I was nervous in meetings, and the way that came out was a compulsive apology in front of anything I said — sorry, this may be a stupid question, sorry, I've probably misunderstood. It was so habitual that I'd have denied doing it.

She took me aside one afternoon, entirely without malice, and asked me why I apologised before I had said a single word. Then she put it in a way I've never quite managed to forget: apologise first and people stop attending to the idea, because they're busy attending to the apology. It was an unpleasant thing to hear, mostly because it was unanswerable.

The remedy was crude. For a couple of months I wrote the word at the top of every page of notes, simply in order to catch myself in the act, and it took until roughly the spring of that year before it stopped surfacing altogether.

What she'd actually done, though, wasn't correct a verbal tic. She'd pointed out that I treated my own opinions as things requiring permission, and once that has been said to you it cannot be unsaid. Which is, I think, what separates advice worth having from the other kind. The useful sort tells you nothing you didn't know; it simply names a habit you were standing too close to see.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a time when I wait very long in the airport. It was two years ago and I am going home for Christmas.

My flight was at seven o'clock in the evening. When I come to the airport, the screen says delayed. Everybody is waiting and nobody tells us anything. After two hours they said the flight is cancelled and we have to wait for another plane in the morning.

So we waited in the airport all the night. There was no hotel and no food after eleven o'clock, only one machine with chocolate in it. I sat on the floor near my bag with an old man from my city and we talked about many things. He was very calm, more calm than me.

Finally at eight o'clock in the morning we went on the plane. It was eleven hours in total.

At the end I was very tired and angry, but also a little bit funny, because now it is a story I tell to my friends. So this is the time when I wait a long time.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a night I spent at an airport a couple of years ago, waiting for a flight home at Christmas.

The flight was supposed to leave at seven in the evening. By the time I got there the board already said delayed, which nobody seemed able to explain, and for the first two hours we just stood around watching it. Then they announced that the flight was cancelled and that we'd be put on something the following morning.

What made it hard wasn't the delay itself. It was that the airport more or less closed around us — the food places shut at eleven, there were no hotel rooms left within an hour's drive, and after midnight there was nobody at any desk to ask. So about sixty of us spent the night on the floor of a departure gate.

I ended up sitting next to a man in his seventies who was travelling to the same city, and we talked, on and off, for about seven hours. He was infinitely calmer about it than I was, which I found slightly annoying at three in the morning and rather admirable by six.

We finally boarded at eight, which made it eleven hours altogether. By that point I was too tired to be angry, and honestly the whole thing has turned into something I rather enjoy telling people about. Which is the odd thing about waiting — it's unbearable while it's happening and it becomes a story about ten minutes after it stops.

what_lifts_it.point: A reported passive, a cleft naming the real difficulty, and a comparative with a full clause.
'Stood around', 'shut at eleven', 'on and off' replace bare adjectives throughout.
One cleft reorganises the middle, and the close abstracts away from the night.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one step further
model_answers.transcript:
The wait I'd describe is a night at an airport a couple of winters ago, for a flight that in the end left thirteen hours late.

It was due out at seven in the evening. The board said delayed from the moment I arrived, with no explanation attached to it, and there is a particular kind of standing about that airports produce — you can't leave, you can't settle, and you can't find anybody to ask. At around nine they cancelled it outright and told us we would be re-booked onto a morning service.

What made the night difficult wasn't the delay so much as the way the building shut down around us. The last food place closed at eleven. Every hotel within an hour was full. From midnight there was not one member of staff on that floor, which meant sixty-odd people were left waiting with nobody to be annoyed at.

I spent most of it beside a man in his seventies heading to the same city, who was so entirely unbothered that I found him irritating at three and rather impressive by six. We boarded a little after eight, thirteen hours after the flight had been due to leave.

I was well past anger by then, and past most other things as well. And it has since become one of those episodes I'm oddly fond of — which is the strange economics of waiting: it costs you everything while it lasts and pays you back afterwards, in stories.

what_lifts_it.point: An existential 'there is a particular kind of' and a 'so ___ that' clause do compound work.
'Standing about', 'sixty-odd', 'well past anger' are spoken rather than written register.
Three short sentences stage the collapse, and the close is a general claim.

teaching.band_move: Report two things the other person actually said. A turn with only your own words in it is a monologue.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a conversation with my neighbour. It happened maybe three years ago in my building, in the winter.

That day there was a power cut in the whole street. It was about six o'clock and it was already dark outside. Nobody has light, so many people go out to the corridor and the stairs with candles and their phones.

I meet there the man who lives above me. Before this, in four years, we only said hello in the lift, that's all. But that evening we talked maybe two hours on the stairs.

He told me many things. He worked before on ships, twenty years, and he saw a lot of countries. Also his wife died five years earlier and now he lives alone. I didn't know anything about this.

Why I remember it? Because he is my neighbour four years and I know nothing about him. It makes me think a lot. Now when I see him we talk properly, not only hello. So this is the conversation which I still remember.

what_caps_it.point: The story slips into the present, the duration has no perfect form, and one question keeps question order.
'Many things', 'a lot of countries', 'properly' — nothing precise anywhere.
Events arrive strictly in order and the close reads the prompt back.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a conversation I had with a neighbour about three years ago, which I still think about rather more than I'd have expected to.

It happened during a power cut, one evening in January. The whole street went dark at about six, and because nobody could do anything indoors, most of the building ended up out on the stairwell with candles and phone torches, waiting for it to come back on.

I got talking to the man who lives directly above me. Up until that evening we'd exchanged nothing but hello in the lift for four years — I couldn't have told you his first name. We ended up sitting on the stairs for the best part of two hours.

He'd spent twenty years at sea, on cargo ships, which I'd had no idea about, and he'd been to places I've only ever read about. And somewhere in the middle of it he mentioned, entirely in passing, that his wife had died five years earlier and that the flat had been very quiet since. He wasn't asking for sympathy about it; he was answering a question I'd put to him.

The reason it's stayed with me isn't really the sailing. It's that I'd lived twelve feet below somebody for four years and had never once found out a single thing about him, and it took a power cut to fix that. We talk properly now — not hello, actual conversations. Which tells you something faintly uncomfortable about how much of a conversation is simply circumstances.

what_lifts_it.point: Past perfect carries all the background, and 'I couldn't have told you' adds a past modal.
'Got talking to', 'entirely in passing', 'the best part of two hours' replace vague nouns.
The fourth bullet is named, and the close makes a claim rather than a summary.

annotations.span: I'll talk about a conversation I had with a neighbour about three years ago
annotations.label: Person and time in the first clause
annotations.why: Two facts in the opening let you spend the rest of the turn on content.

annotations.span: I got talking to the man who lives directly above me
annotations.label: The exact chunk for an unplanned start
annotations.why: 'Get talking to' means it wasn't arranged, which is the whole point here.

annotations.span: Up until that evening we'd exchanged nothing but hello in the lift for four years
annotations.label: Past perfect covering four years
annotations.why: One 'we'd ___ for ___' sentence does all the background at once.

annotations.span: I couldn't have told you his first name
annotations.label: Past modal proving the point
annotations.why: 'I couldn't have told you ___' is stronger than 'I didn't know him well'.

annotations.span: entirely in passing
annotations.label: Two words describe how it was said
annotations.why: Saying how something was mentioned is more informative than the mention.

annotations.span: that his wife had died five years earlier
annotations.label: Past perfect plus 'earlier', not 'before'
annotations.why: Inside a past story, use 'earlier' or 'previously' rather than 'before'.

annotations.span: The reason it's stayed with me isn't really the sailing.
annotations.label: Announces the last bullet and reframes
annotations.why: Saying what it isn't about buys you a whole sentence and sounds considered.

annotations.span: it took a power cut to fix that
annotations.label: 'It took X to Y' delivers the irony
annotations.why: The structure lets a small cause carry a large consequence.

annotations.span: how much of a conversation is simply circumstances
annotations.label: Closes on a general claim
annotations.why: End above the story; it is the cheapest lift available in the last ten seconds.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one step further
model_answers.transcript:
The conversation I'd pick took place on a staircase during a power cut, three winters ago, and it went on for something like two hours.

The whole street lost power at six on a January evening and, since there was nothing to be done indoors, most of the building drifted out onto the landings with candles and phones. Among them was the man from the flat directly above mine, with whom, in four years, I had exchanged precisely nothing beyond a nod in the lift.

We sat on the stairs and talked until the lights came back. It emerged that he'd spent two decades at sea on cargo ships and had been to half the ports I've only ever read about, and that his wife had died five years earlier — which he mentioned in the same tone he'd been using for the shipping. He wasn't seeking sympathy. He was answering what I'd asked.

What has stayed with me isn't the biography. It's that I had lived twelve feet beneath a man for four years without discovering one thing about him, and that it took a failure of the electricity supply to correct that. We speak properly now, which is its own small indictment.

I've since come round to the view that most conversations which never happen aren't prevented by dislike, or even by shyness. They're prevented by there never being an occasion — and occasions turn out to be remarkably easy to arrange.

what_lifts_it.point: 'With whom' and 'it emerged that' compress background band 7 spread over three sentences.
'Drifted out', 'its own small indictment', 'come round to the view' choose register deliberately.
The close states a general position about conversation instead of summarising the evening.

annotations.span: with whom, in four years, I had exchanged precisely nothing beyond a nod in the lift
annotations.label: Relative clause with a fronted preposition
annotations.why: 'With whom' is worth having for exactly one sentence per turn.

annotations.span: It emerged that he'd spent two decades at sea on cargo ships
annotations.label: 'It emerged that' introduces reported facts
annotations.why: The structure lets you report several facts without saying 'he told me' repeatedly.

annotations.span: which he mentioned in the same tone he'd been using for the shipping
annotations.label: Describes the delivery, not the content
annotations.why: Noting how something was said is the most transferable observation here.

annotations.span: He wasn't seeking sympathy. He was answering what I'd asked.
annotations.label: Two short parallel sentences
annotations.why: Matching rhythm across two short sentences makes the contrast audible.

annotations.span: it took a failure of the electricity supply to correct that
annotations.label: Formal register used for dry effect
annotations.why: Deliberately over-formal wording is a joke a native speaker would make.

annotations.span: They're prevented by there never being an occasion
annotations.label: Names the real obstacle at the close
annotations.why: Explaining the cause rather than deploring the effect is the band-8 finish.
